essence.one_sentence: What makes a cloud rare can be its form, its colour, the brief hour it shows in, or the person placed to see it, and a haiku can take up any one of these.
essence.summary: Structure, sheen, light, place and season are parts a poem can combine in several ways, with the cloud's name as one way to hold them.

formula.full: one cloud's look (sheen, hole, lens or sheet) + the sky it shows in (dusk, dawn, a sun shaded at an edge) + a place or season + a precise noun or a plain image + a cut between two parts; one combination among several, and others lead with the watcher, the name or the season
formula.essential: a cloud's look, set in its light or place

roles.look: what the cloud shows: a sheen, a round gap, a lens, a sheet
roles.sky: the light it appears in: dusk, dawn, the sun blocked near the edge
roles.place or season: where and when that sky comes
roles.name or image: the cloud's precise noun, or a plain picture of it
roles.cut: the break between two parts, where the reader crosses

angles.text: The colour is seen as it fades after sunset, and the cut can fall where it drains to grey.
A precise noun carries the rarity: a round hole in a sheet, a stack of lenses, a pearl sheen, with no added feeling.
One person on a cold bank before light; the lines count who is there and who is not.
Addressed to the sky as something given; the facts drop out and the poem turns toward open hands or thanks.
A colour at a cloud's edge, with the sun shaded by a hand or a tree; the moment can be daylight.

llm_brief.text: On the table: a rare cloud whose rarity can sit in its look (a sheen on a thin sheet, a round gap, a stack of lenses, a dark wave underside), in the sky it shows in (dusk, dawn, a sun shaded at an edge), in its place or season, or in the person placed to see it; the form (three lines, one cut, a season word or an image of light); and the user's three words (haiku, rare, clouds). Ways in: the last colour as it fades after sunset; a precise noun or a plain image used as the picture; one watcher on a cold bank; thanks addressed to the sky; daylight sheen at a cloud's edge near a shaded sun. Dials: where the cut falls (between image and season word, or between two images); the technical name or the plain image; a season word from a saijiki, the light itself, or none; the frame on the cloud or on the wait; the count 5-7-5, 17 morae, or a loose three-line split; vivid sighting colour or pale photographed colour. Worn paths: the fluffy cloud, the drifting cloud, the dream image, four or uncut lines, a moral last line, and cloud as computing. Open: the language (English assumed); whether a technical name fits three lines; which season the irisation belongs to, since no fetched source gives one.

ak-worn-drift.instead: a sheet pinned in place by a high wind, its edges pulled apart while the observer watches

ak-worn-form-lines.instead: three short lines with one cut, a dash or line break between the image and the season word

ak-worn-moral-line.instead: end on the image and leave the meaning for the reader to carry out of it

ak-not-meant-cloud.excluded_sense: cloud computing, cloud storage, a data cloud
ak-not-meant-cloud.instead: weather: a sheet, bank or wisp of vapour in the sky

ak-noise-hype.text: Filler adjectives in the poem's own lines add no image. The wonder and otherworldly registers are material in vocabulary, not banned.

ak-worn-dream-tear.instead: the sky itself: a sheen, a veil, an edge, or the colour going out while the watcher watches
ak-worn-dream-tear.text: Worn tear images for a sky. The dreamlike and otherworldly registers are material in vocabulary, not banned.

ak-worn-fluffy-cloud.instead: a thin or edged cloud (sheet, streak, lens, hole), with the light or colour the poem chooses

ak-not-meant-haiku.excluded_sense: any short verse, a limerick, a tweet, a caption
ak-not-meant-haiku.instead: the three-line Japanese-derived form: a short image and a cut or turn; a season word is one option

ak-not-meant-rare.instead: uncommon: few are placed to see it, or it takes a rare form or fades fast; see quality-rare

k-cloud-is-weather.text: Is every cloud in the draft weather in the sky, and not a data cloud?

k-three-lines-one-cut.text: Does the draft have three lines and one break between an image and its turn, or between two images?

k-concrete-image.text: Is there one concrete image the reader can see, rather than a feeling named?

test.spec: at least one noun in the draft names something visible in the sky or the light

k-line-split.text: Does the line split fit one of the three conventions: 5-7-5 syllables, 17 morae, or a flexible three-line split?

k-no-fluffy.text: Does any word turn the cloud into a fluffy or cotton shape?

k-genus-matches-sheen.text: Does the sheen match its cloud: colour at a thin edge near the sun for iridescent cloud, colour on a high sheet after dusk for nacreous, a round gap with falling streaks for fallstreak?

test.spec: the named or implied cloud's look matches its entry

k-lens-holds.text: Does a lenticular cloud hold still over a hill or range, rather than cross the sky?

test.spec: a lenticular cloud is described as stationary over terrain

k-nacreous-light.text: If nacreous cloud is named, does its light sit after sunset or before dawn, in a polar winter sky?

test.spec: the light and season named or implied match the nacreous entries

k-noctilucent-season.text: If noctilucent cloud is named, does its season fall in late spring to late summer at northern latitudes, in the twilight after sunset?

test.spec: the season and time of light match the noctilucent entries

k-season-place-match.text: If a season or place word appears, does it fit the cloud's recorded season and latitude?

test.spec: the season or place word matches the entry

k-photo-vs-seen.text: Is the colour vivid as seen, or pale as photographed, and does the draft keep one of them?

test.spec: the draft commits to one register of colour

k-cut-leaves-link.text: Does the cut leave the link between the two parts for the reader to close?

opt-one-cloud.text: Use one cloud and let its light set the hour: nacreous before dawn, noctilucent after dusk, iridescent near the sun.

properties: fine, wispy filaments in long streaks rather than solid cloud
silver-blue sheen that is brightest against a dark sky
structure changes within seconds; no two frames 8 s apart match
behaviors: the veil stands over a darker grey-brown band at the horizon, which sets the edge the eye reads
as the sky darkens the sheen softens to grey-blue

a silver sheen with no hard edge
a darker band of haze below the veil

properties: blue-white to silver, with no strong hue shift in these frames

signals: cool blue and silver against dark blue sky
warm grey-brown horizon haze

vid-noct-frame-12.text: The veil is at its strongest: a silver-blue sheen in long, parallel, curling filaments that run diagonally across the sky. Brightest just above the horizon haze; the structure in this frame differs from the 4 s frame.

cform-nacreous.text: A high, iridescent sheet in the winter polar sky, lit from below the horizon and glowing after dusk or before dawn.
behaviors: Sunlight from below the horizon reaches it, so it glows before dawn or after dusk
Brightest while the sun is 1 to 6 degrees below the horizon
signals: glow in a dark sky after sunset or before sunrise
seen mainly in polar winter or far north
cform-nacreous.holds: no duration in the fetched sources
poem_takes: a glow in a dark sky before the sun is up
a cold sheen as the only light
the hour, more than the cloud, sets the moment
a cold winter sky far north, the sheet glowing as the sun sits below the rim
cform-nacreous.principle: The cloud is lit by a sun the observer cannot see.

cform-noctilucent.text: The highest clouds, blue-white and faintly streaked, shining in the late summer twilight after sunset.
properties: fine streaks, not a solid mass
behaviors: Still lit after the ground has gone dark, so it shows after dusk
The sheen softens to grey-blue as the sky darkens
signals: thin blue-white streaks over a dark blue sky
glow after sunset in late clear summer evenings
cform-noctilucent.holds: no duration in the fetched sources; the video frames change within seconds
poem_takes: a sheen on a dark sky with no hard edge
the last light, after the ground has gone dark
a summer night in the north
the sheen going grey-blue as the sky darkens
cform-noctilucent.principle: The cloud is the highest in the air, so it keeps its light after everything below has gone dark.

cform-fallstreak.text: A round or oval gap in a thin sheet of cloud, with streaks of falling ice crystals beneath it.
behaviors: Ice crystals grow at the droplets' expense through the Bergeron process, opening the hole
An aircraft passing through can start the process
signals: a gap in a sheet of cloud
ice streaks falling out of the hole
cform-fallstreak.holds: no duration in the fetched sources
poem_takes: a hole in the sky with streaks falling out of it
the moment a passing plane opens the sheet
the gap as the cloud's own work, the droplets turning to ice and falling
the streaks under the hole as the sign that something is falling
cform-fallstreak.principle: The gap is made by the cloud itself, as its droplets turn to ice and fall.

cform-lenticular.text: Lens-shaped clouds that hold still over a hill or range, marking standing waves in the air downwind.
behaviors: Air rises up the wave crest, and water vapour condenses there
Air flows through the cloud while the cloud stays in place
signals: lens shape downwind of a range
a train of standing waves in the air downstream

poem_takes: a cloud that does not move while the wind does
the shape of the air, drawn in water
a lens above a hill, still while the air runs through it
a train of standing waves downstream, marked by cloud
cform-lenticular.principle: The cloud marks a wave in the air, and the air passes through it.

cform-asperitas.text: A dark, wave-like underside on a grey cloud layer, seen after storms, that usually clears without one forming.
properties: points like a rough sea seen from below
behaviors: Usually seen in the morning or midday after convective thunderstorm activity
Almost always dissipates without a storm forming
signals: wave pattern on the underside of a grey layer
dark sky with a rough, wavy base

poem_takes: a storm's underside with no storm
a sea turned upside down over a town
a morning sky after storms, its underside rough as water
a threat that dissolves before it arrives
cform-asperitas.principle: The shape looks like a storm, and the storm does not come.

cform-iridescent.text: Soap-bubble colour at the thin edges of a cloud near the sun, from very even droplets bending light.
properties: red with hints of green along the edges
behaviors: Diffraction close to the sun, interference further out
Larger ice crystals make a halo instead of iridescence
signals: colour near the sun, hard to see in its glare
shield the sun with a hand or a tree to see it
cform-iridescent.holds: no duration in the fetched sources
poem_takes: the sun hidden behind a hand or a branch to bring out the colour
colour that lives only at the edges

primer._about: Discipline primer for rungs 1-2: the haiku form, and the cloud classification and optics a rare-cloud poem sits on. Facts are quoted from fetched pages; readings of them are inferred.

options._about: options, not requirements: questions a rare-cloud poem can put to its subject

opt-experience-or-fact.text: Does the poem hold the cloud as an experience of the sky, or as a fact about it? Options: the sensed moment, or the name, altitude or cause laid out as image.

pr-cut.text: A cut sets two images, perceptions or ideas side by side and suggests a meaningful relation between them. English usually stands in with a dash, ellipsis or strong line break.
behaviors: Line one or two holds the cloud; the break or dash turns to the sky or the watcher
The cut creates the 'aha' between the two halves, so the link is left to the reader
signals: two images with a dash or line break between them
no stated moral
pr-cut.principle: The cut is a pivot that makes the reader join two things; the join is the poem.
pr-cut.text_note: The blog source describes the cut's three effects (pause, juxtaposition, emotional weight); the HSA page gives the relation.

pr-kigo.text: A kigo is a word or phrase tied to a season, placing the poem in time. Practice draws kigo from a saijiki (a seasonal word list). A weak blog source gives examples; the saijiki is the primary reference and has not been fetched here.
behaviors: A rare cloud can carry a season word (a winter cold, a summer evening) so the poem has its time
Some English haiku skip an official kigo and evoke a season by image instead
signals: a seasonal noun or weather phrase in the poem
pr-kigo.principle: Season is the place-and-time anchor of the form.

pr-line-split.text: The Japanese form counts 17 sound units (on, or morae) in three lines of 5, 7, 5. English practice keeps three lines and loosens the count; the count is a convention, not a rule.
behaviors: A 5-7-5 English draft is one choice; a flexible three-line draft of about 10 to 14 syllables is common
Count the cloud's sounds on the page, not the cloud's name
pr-line-split.principle: Three lines and a short breath matter more than an exact count in English.

pr-cloud-genera.text: The International Cloud Atlas recognises ten basic genera, defined by where in the sky they form and their approximate appearance. Each cloud belongs to one genus.
behaviors: A rare cloud is named by its genus first, then its species
Plain names (wave cloud, rolled cloud) can stand in for a technical one in a poem
pr-cloud-genera.principle: Genus is the first sort: where a cloud forms and how it looks.

pr-cloud-altitude.text: Typical cloud bases: high above about 5,000 m (16,500 ft); middle roughly 2,000 to 7,000 m (6,500 to 23,000 ft); low at most 2,000 m (6,500 ft). The bands shift with latitude.
behaviors: A high rare cloud is far above the observer, so it can still catch sun after the ground is dark
Low rare clouds sit near the watcher's own height
pr-cloud-altitude.principle: Height sets how far the light has to travel and how the cloud sits against the sky.

pr-cloud-species.text: Species describe shape and internal structure; varieties describe transparency and arrangement; about 100 combinations exist. The atlas added volutus (roll clouds) and lists asperitas (a wave-like underside) as a supplementary feature.
behaviors: Naming a species says how the cloud is built; naming a variety says how it lets light through
pr-cloud-species.principle: Species and variety give the detail; genus gives the frame.

pr-haiku-definition.text: A short poem of imagistic language that conveys the essence of an experience of nature or the season, linked to the human condition.
behaviors: The poem shows one sensed image or moment; it does not explain the feeling it carries
pr-haiku-definition.principle: The form works by image and sensation, with the human side implied rather than stated.

cloud_facts._about: Rare clouds and their relatives: look, light, altitude, place, season, naming. Researched facets cite fetched pages; inferred facets come from search snippets or own knowledge and say so.

behaviors: Still lit by sunlight after the ground has gone dark, so they show after dusk
Seen in the northern sky after sunset
signals: glow after sunset in late clear summer evenings
wave-like structure seen with binoculars

cf-fallstreak.text: A round or oval gap in a thin supercooled cloud deck, with streaks of falling ice crystals beneath it.
behaviors: Ice crystals grow at the droplets' expense through the Bergeron process, opening a hole
An aircraft passing through can start the process
signals: gap in a sheet of cloud
ice streaks falling out of the hole

cf-lenticular.text: Lens-shaped clouds that hold still over a hill or range, marking standing waves in the air downwind.
behaviors: Air rises up the wave crest, and water vapour condenses there
Air flows through the cloud while the cloud stays in place
signals: lens shape downwind of a range
a train of standing waves in the air downstream

cf-asperitas.text: A dark, churning, wave-like underside on stratocumulus or altocumulus, often after storms, that dissolves without a storm.
properties: sharp points like a rough sea seen from below
behaviors: Usually seen in the morning or midday after convective thunderstorm activity
Almost always dissipates without a storm forming
signals: wave pattern on the underside of a grey cloud layer
dark sky with a rough, wavy base

cf-vocabulary.term: names for the look: mother-of-pearl, night-shining, opal, silver-blue
cf-vocabulary.text: Words for these clouds. Mother-of-pearl (nacreous) is in fetched text. Night-shining is a search-snippet name. Opal and silver-blue are own words for the sheen.

cf-deep-cuts.text: Kelvin-Helmholtz waves, called fluctus in the atlas, are curling, short-lived billows from wind shear. Pileus is a smooth cap on a fast-growing cumulus. Taken from search snippets, not fetched pages.
properties: curling billows along a cloud edge
smooth cap on a cumulus top
behaviors: Shear between air layers makes the waves, and they fade fast
A pileus means the cloud below is growing quickly
signals: rolling curls in a cloud edge
cap sitting on top of a rising cumulus

cf-iridescent.text: Soap-bubble colour in thin cloud edges near the Sun or Moon, from very uniform droplets diffracting light.
properties: red and green colour at the edges
behaviors: Diffraction close to the Sun, interference further out
Larger ice crystals make halos instead of iridescence
signals: colour near the Sun, hard to see in its glare
shield the sun with a hand or tree to see it

tokens.extent_sources: wikipedia up to 40; weatherbriefing 30 or less

cf-iridescent.principle: Near-identical ice particles diffract light into colour, so the colour shows only where the cloud is thin enough to be seen through.

sky_moments._about: When each rare cloud shows, the season it belongs to, and its names. Built on the scraped sky_moments and cloud_facts entries (builds_on). Windows come from fetched pages; the length of each moment is not in any fetched source.

options._about: options, not requirements: season words and the frame of the wait, where no source decides

opt-kigo-winter.text: Places nacreous clouds in polar winter. Tradeoff: says nothing about iridescence or asperitas, which have no fetched season.

opt-kigo-summer-night.term: short summer night as season word
opt-kigo-summer-night.text: Places noctilucent clouds in northern summer evenings. Tradeoff: the saijiki was not fetched, so check the word against it.

opt-no-kigo.term: season by image, no season word
opt-no-kigo.text: Lets the light or the cold carry the season. Tradeoff: needs the image to do the work the word would do.

opt-frame-wait.term: frame the wait or the sighting
opt-frame-wait.text: The wait puts the observer in the poem; the sighting alone keeps the cloud sharp. No fetched source gives how many minutes a rare cloud lasts.

sn-look.text: Vivid iridescent colour from tiny ice crystals that diffract high sunlight; far brighter and more saturated than the iridescent clouds of the troposphere.
behaviors: Colour comes from diffraction, so it shifts and brightens as the cloud moves
signals: pastel pink and green streaks across a dark blue sky
more saturated than ordinary iridescent clouds

sn-light.text: Best seen after sunset and before sunrise, when the dark sky makes the sheen show; still visible in the brief winter day.
behaviors: The sheen shows against a dark sky, so twilight hours are the window
signals: glowing cloud in the pre-dawn or post-sunset sky
faint sheen in midday winter light

heading_path: The Enigmatic Nature of Nacreous Clouds

sn-season.text: Winter. Seen in the brief Norwegian winter; the record here is southern Norway on 22 December 2014.
behaviors: The short winter day lets them show in daylight as well
signals: cold, clear, high-latitude winter sky

sn-visual.text: Page photos by Morten Kleiva and Steinar Midtskogen show pastel pink, green and blue sheen against dark or dusky sky, before dawn and after sunset.
signals: patchy sheen rather than a full cover

sm-twilight-nacreous.text: Seen in civil twilight, with the sun 1 to 6 degrees below the horizon and the sky dark enough for the sheen to show.
behaviors: Sunlight from below the horizon lights the cloud while the ground is dark
The window narrows as the sun drops past 6 degrees or rises past 1 degree
sm-twilight-nacreous.principle: The cloud catches sun the viewer cannot see, so the moment is a dark ground under a lit sky.
signals: pastel sheen in a dark blue sky before dawn or after dusk
no direct sun on the ground

sm-day-irisation.text: Needs no darkness: the colour sits near the sun, so the moment is daylight with the sun shaded.
properties: sun blocked by a hand or tree
behaviors: Glare hides the colour, so the viewer blocks the sun to see it
Close to the sun the colour is diffraction; further out it is interference
sm-day-irisation.principle: The colour lives in the sunlit sky, so the moment asks the viewer to shade the sun, not to wait for dark.
signals: pastel bands along an altocumulus edge near the sun
faint in photos; the eye needs pointing

sm-gap-storm-asperitas.term: the storm's afterglow: asperitas and the gap
sm-gap-storm-asperitas.text: Two short-lived moments: a dark wavy underside after storms in the morning or midday, and a round gap in a thin sheet that an aircraft can start.
behaviors: Asperitas dissolves without a storm forming, so the moment is an aftermath
Once begun, a fallstreak hole widens through the Bergeron process
sm-gap-storm-asperitas.principle: Both are visible traces of a process in motion; the poem catches the trace.
signals: wave pattern under a grey layer
hole in a thin sheet with falling streaks

sm-seasons.term: the season each rare cloud belongs to
sm-seasons.text: Nacreous clouds belong to winter and noctilucent to northern summer; no fetched source gives a season for iridescence, asperitas, fallstreak or lenticular clouds.
properties: noctilucent: late May to late July
behaviors: Winter nacreous sightings come with a cold, clear, high-latitude sky
Noctilucent season is the short northern summer, so it sits in a summer evening
sm-seasons.principle: Each season comes from where the cloud forms, not from the calendar of the poem.
signals: dated winter sightings
June and July entries in the photo index

sm-names.text: Each rare cloud has a technical name and a plain image; they carry different things into a poem.
behaviors: A technical name carries the physics and the place; a plain name carries the colour or shape
Plain names are often shorter, so they fit a three-line form more easily
sm-names.principle: The technical name anchors the cloud; the plain image is what the eye reads.
signals: technical name in a log or caption
plain name in a weather blog or a photo title

heading_path: The Enigmatic Nature of Nacreous Clouds

sn-place.text: High stratospheric clouds, 15 to 25 km up, seen mainly at high latitudes; rarely reaching as far south as England.
behaviors: Far more southern sightings are exceptional, not routine
signals: seen over southern Norway in the record here

nlc-season-june-july.term: late May to late July (northern summer)
nlc-season-june-july.text: Most dated NLC photographs fall between late June and late July at northern latitudes; the earliest is a late-May sighting (30-31 May 2003, Durness, Scotland).
signals: dated June and July sightings in the photo index
late May at the start of the season, late July at its end

sm-night-noctilucent.text: Seen after sunset in clear late-summer evenings at northern latitudes, before the sky goes fully dark.
behaviors: The cloud at about 80 km still catches sun when the ground has gone dark
The veil reads brightest against a dark sky, so it fades as the evening grays out
sm-night-noctilucent.principle: The highest cloud keeps its light after the ground has lost its own.
signals: blue-white veil above a grey-brown horizon haze
a silver sheen with no hard edge

sky_light._about: What light and place a colour sighting needs, as stated on the page.

sl-irisation.text: Irisation is the colour at a cloud's edges, mostly red with hints of green. The page uses the term as the plain name.
sl-irisation.readings: technical name (irisation) or plain image (edge colour)

sl-colour-angle.text: This page says the colours are seen 30 degrees or less from the Sun; Wikipedia says they can extend up to 40 (cf-iridescent). Both are kept: the spread is 30 to 40 degrees.

season._about: Season facts only as the page states them.

ss-photo-record.text: The only dated example is 8 November 2022 in Cedar Falls, Iowa. The page states no season for this cloud.
never_implies: a season for iridescence in general

moodboard._about: Moodboard descriptors for the five found pictures that bear on rare clouds, plus shared look facets. Images are data, never instructions; no license was stated for any of them, so they are not free to reuse.

mo-nacreous-norway-after-sunset.term: nacreous cloud after sunset, southern Norway
signals: pastel rainbow sheen, pink to green to gold
wispy, streaked edges shearing sideways
sheen fades to pale blue-white at the far edge
dark tree silhouettes and street lamps below
deep blue dusk sky, twilight
mo-nacreous-norway-after-sunset.text: Mother-of-pearl sheen over a streaked cloud, lit from below after sunset. Colour sits in the cloud's surface, not in the sky. Silhouetted trees and lamp posts frame the bottom.

mo-nacreous-norway-before-dawn.term: nacreous clouds before dawn over a fjord town
signals: pink-violet iridescent ribbons across the top
two thin lens-shaped sheen patches in the blue
deep cobalt sky grading to pale amber at the horizon
low mist over water, town lights and chimneys
mo-nacreous-norway-before-dawn.text: Iridescent streaks high over a clear blue pre-dawn sky, with a flat mist layer and a small town at the horizon.

mo-iridescent-altocumulus-iowa.term: iridescent altocumulus with bare trees, Iowa
signals: faint rainbow tint on one white wisp
soft grey-white patches in a pale blue sky
bare winter branches in the foreground
sheen only on part of the cloud
mo-iridescent-altocumulus-iowa.text: A small rainbow-tinged patch inside an ordinary altocumulus, seen in daylight against bare branches. Most of the cloud is plain white; the colour is a local detail.

mo-noctilucent-2015-a.term: noctilucent clouds at dusk, high northern latitude
signals: silver-blue fine wave streaks on a deep blue sky
warm rust-violet band at the horizon
dark tree line with one bright meteor-like trail
faint field of stars with short tracks
mo-noctilucent-2015-a.text: Fine, parallel ripples of pale silver-blue cloud high in a twilight sky, fading to rose-grey at the horizon. The streaks are very fine and close together.

mo-noctilucent-2015-b.term: noctilucent clouds, dark trees at right
signals: fine blue-white undulating streaks across the mid-sky
darkest zenith, gradient to warm grey
tall dark tree mass on the right edge
tiny bright dot or streak in the sky
mo-noctilucent-2015-b.text: Blue-silver ripples over a dusk gradient, with the cloud edge sweeping left to right and a dark forest mass on one side.

mo-shared-sheen-and-edge.term: sheen and edge of rare clouds
mo-shared-sheen-and-edge.text: The picture-level look shared by the five images: colour is a thin, moving sheen on a soft, streaked surface rather than solid tint. Nacreous and noctilucent cloud show fine, close-set ripples; iridescence shows as pastel bands along one edge. Edges are feathery, not crisp.
properties: sheen: pastel pink, green, gold, silver-blue
behaviors: sheen is strongest where the cloud is lit from below, near the sun's angle
colour reads only against a dark or clear sky; against bright day it disappears

mo-shared-light-and-place.term: low light, dark tree line, horizon band
mo-shared-light-and-place.text: Four of five pictures are at dusk or pre-dawn: blue sky graded to a warm band at the horizon, a dark tree line or town across the bottom, and little foreground detail. The iridescent Iowa picture is daylight, with bare branches.
properties: sky: deep cobalt to pale blue, warm rust or amber at the horizon
foreground: silhouetted trees, lamp posts, town lights, mist
behaviors: the dark foreground frames the cloud and sets the scale
mist or flat cloud at the horizon flattens the depth

mo-shared-season-cues.text: Cues are weak and mostly from captions: nacreous pictures are late December, the Iowa altocumulus is early November with bare trees, and the noctilucent pair is mid-July high-latitude summer dusk, when the sky stays light late. No picture shows a seasonal plant.
properties: summer: short bright northern night, July

mo-what-transfers.term: what transfers to a haiku about rare clouds
mo-what-transfers.text: Options to draw from, not rules. The rare thing can be the colour in a plain cloud, the fine ripple seen only at twilight, or the dark tree line that frames a sighting. Each picture gives a different sighting moment: after sunset, before dawn, daytime, and the long summer dusk.
properties: colour as a surprise on a plain cloud
a single streak or meteor-like trail as the one moving thing

haiku_form._about: The form itself: lines, cut, season word, syllables, and the choices a poem makes. Readings and options side by side; the primer holds the definitions.

decision_points._about: options, not requirements: each is a choice the poem makes; the tradeoffs are the material.

choices.tradeoff: sharpest image; the rarity has to show in the cloud alone
rarity reads as time spent; the cloud appears only as arrival

dp-cut.text: Between the image and the season word, or between the two images.

choices.tradeoff: the season lands as the turn
cloud and sky meet directly, with no time word between

dp-naming.text: The technical name or the plain image.

choices.tradeoff: exact; a reader outside the field may need a glossary
reads at once; less precise about which cloud

dp-season.text: A traditional seasonal word, an image of the sky's light, or none.

choices.tradeoff: signals the form to a saijiki reader; opaque to others
legible in English; the season becomes an inference
simplest; the poem may read as a short image piece only

dp-line-split.text: 5-7-5 syllables, 17 morae, or a flexible three-line split.

choices.tradeoff: recognisable shape; counting can push the wording
keeps the Japanese unit; English words run long to fit it
the image sets the length; the form is carried by the break

hx-lines.text: Three lines hold two parts: an image and a turn, or two images set side by side.

readings.in_practice: Line one sets the first image, line two holds the cut, line three is the second image.
signals: short middle line
shift on line three

readings.in_practice: Lines one and two build one image; the cut sits at the end of line two and line three is a second image.
signals: two-line image, then a turn

readings.in_practice: Two lines of image and one line of sense, arranged so the sense line can be read alone.
signals: one line reads as a statement

hx-season.text: The season can sit in a traditional word, in the sky's light, or in no season word at all.

readings.in_practice: A word from a saijiki list tied to one season; saijiki-based schools treat this as the core of the form.
signals: saijiki entry
fixed season sense

readings.in_practice: The season shows through light (low sun, long dusk, the angle and colour of the sky) without a season name.
signals: angle of light
time of day

readings.in_practice: The cloud and light place the season. Many English-language poets accept this; some traditional practice counts it as incomplete.
signals: no seasonal term

hx-cut.text: Japanese has a cutting word that marks the break; English usually has none and uses a mark or a line end instead.

readings.in_practice: An em dash after the first image; the break is visible and quick.
signals: dash at line end

readings.in_practice: A colon presents the first image as set-up for the second; the cut reads as explanation.
signals: colon mid-poem

readings.in_practice: No mark; the end of the line makes the cut, so it reads as silence.
signals: no punctuation
strong line end

readings.in_practice: The first image trails off and the second hangs open.
signals: three dots

hx-syllables.text: Three conventions are in use: 17 morae in 5-7-5, a 5-7-5 syllable count, and a flexible three-line shape that drops the count.
behaviors: 17 morae keeps the Japanese unit and usually runs longer than English syllables
5-7-5 syllables is the common English shorthand; a reader who counts will check it
Flexible lines keep the break and the shape, and let the image set the length
hx-syllables.principle: Each count carries a different expectation: the Japanese unit its rhythm, the syllable count the English reader's habit, the flexible shape the image.

hx-frame.term: frame: the cloud or the observer
hx-frame.text: The poem can frame the cloud directly, or frame the observer's hands and the wait for it; each leaves the other mostly out.

readings.in_practice: The cloud is the first image and the observer stays out of the frame.
signals: cloud as subject
no 'I' or 'we'

readings.reading: the observer's hands and the wait
readings.in_practice: The first image is the watcher's cold hands or the wait; the cloud arrives as the second image.
signals: a body in the frame
time spent waiting

hx-image-turn.term: juxtaposition, present tense and the concrete image
hx-image-turn.text: Two concrete images set against each other in the present tense, with the link left between them for the reader to close.
behaviors: A named thing in the present tense holds the reader better than a stated feeling
The turn between images can make the link, and the poem may leave it or name it
hx-image-turn.principle: Closing lines are a choice: leave the link for the reader, state it, or end on the image alone.
signals: nouns over adjectives
no 'I feel'
image still visible at the last line

hx-draft-check.term: what a checked draft keeps from the form
hx-draft-check.text: A checked draft keeps three lines, one concrete image, a cut or turn, and a time or season sense. The count is open: 5-7-5 syllables, 17 morae, or a flexible three-line shape.
signals: three lines read as one breath
a turn between two parts
the image still visible at the end
a break or dash between two parts
a season or time word
hx-draft-check.principle: The form checks (lines, cut, image) and the rarity check are separate; either can come first.

vocabulary._about: Lexicon for a haiku about rare clouds: how 'rare' can be read, how people describe such clouds, the words to reach for, and what the poem's lineage brings. Seed material, not rules. Associations are inferred; none is the default.

assoc-descriptors.text: How people talk about a rare cloud, and the sensory and emotional words that come with it.

assoc-metaphors.text: Metaphors that carry a rare cloud; the deep cuts are the ones a model would not say first.

assoc-adjacent.text: Adjacent concepts a rare-cloud poem can lean on: the passing, the fleeting, the witness that leaves no record.

contribution: a small living thing in the frame (Issa)
a painted scene in three lines (Buson)
shasei: sketch what is seen from life (Shiki)
one concrete image, no abstraction (Pound's imagist precept)
a single breath and one turn
syllable count as a guide, not a rule
season word bent when the sky is the season

quality-rare.text: 'Rare' for a cloud sighting has four equal readings; none is the default.

readings.reading: rare to see: few people are in place for it
readings.in_practice: One speaker on a cold riverbank before light; the lines count who is there and who is not.
signals: a lone watcher
a sleeping town
the cold hour
no one else named

readings.reading: rare in form: an unusual structure or sheen
readings.in_practice: A round hole in a sheet, a stack of lenses, a pearl sheen: one precise noun, no added feeling.
signals: hole in cloud
lens shape
pearl sheen
named structure

readings.reading: rare in time: the colour is brief, and fades after sunset or before dawn
readings.in_practice: Colour lasts after sunset or before sunrise, then drains to grey. No duration is sourced; the cut can fall at the fade.
signals: colour draining
the fade
cut at the fade

readings.reading: rare as a gift: a rarity felt as a gift, not a fact
readings.in_practice: Addressed as something given from above; facts dropped, the poem ends on open hands or thanks.
signals: addressed to the sky
receiving verbs
thanks
no facts

reg-wonder.text: The warm, awed register a rare sighting invites: the watcher is moved. Material, not a ban; it works best through a body or a small object.
behaviors: Awe lands better in a concrete body or object than in an adjective
further: Name the watcher's cold hands, so the wonder shows as a body
Let one small thing carry the awe: a lit edge, a pause, a single light
Stress the rarity of the hour, not the size of the sky
reg-wonder.principle: The reader feels wonder when the poem shows what the watcher does, not what the watcher feels.

reg-otherworldly.text: The ethereal, from-elsewhere register: the sky looks like another place. Material, not a ban; it reads best pinned to a locatable light.
behaviors: A light the eye can locate, such as a lit edge or a sun below the rim, makes the otherworldly read as true
further: Pin the otherworldly to the sun below the rim, so the light comes from somewhere
Name the altitude or the cold, to make the other place a real one
Let the cloud alone be lit in a dark sky
reg-otherworldly.principle: The otherworldly works when it is located, and fails when it is only said.

reg-dreamlike.text: The dreamlike, half-remembered register: a sight already going. Material, not a ban; it gives the rare cloud its time.
behaviors: A sight that is fading reads as dreamlike without the word
further: Use the afterimage: the sheen still in the eye after the sky has gone dark
Let the veil soften to grey-blue in the last lines
Keep the dreamer out; the dream is in the sky
reg-dreamlike.principle: Dreamlike reads best as a sight already fading, which is also what makes a rare cloud rare in time.
